requirements.requirement: PostgreSQL streaming replication installed and configured across node1, node2, node3
requirements.summary: PostgreSQL 16 installed and verified via dpkg -l on all three nodes.

requirements.requirement: node1 configured as the writable primary (wal_level, listen_addresses, replication role, pg_hba, replication slots)
requirements.summary: postgresql.conf shows wal_level=replica, listen_addresses='*', max_wal_senders/max_replication_slots set, hot_standby=on. Replicator role created with SCRAM auth, pg_hba.conf entries added for node2/node3, physical replication slots created, service restarted and confirmed active.

requirements.requirement: node2 and node3 provisioned as read-only standbys via base backup from the primary
requirements.summary: pg_basebackup ran to completion (100%) on both nodes after an initial slot-conflict error was self-corrected; postgresql.auto.conf shows primary_conninfo pointing to node1 and standby.signal is present on both nodes.

requirements.requirement: Standbys are read-only and actively streaming from the primary
requirements.summary: pg_is_in_recovery() returns true on node2/node3; pg_stat_replication on node1 shows both nodes in 'streaming' state with slots active.

requirements.requirement: Changes committed on the primary are visible on both standbys; standbys reject writes
requirements.summary: A row inserted on node1 (repl_test id=1) was observed via SELECT on both node2 and node3 within seconds; direct INSERT attempts on both standbys failed with 'cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction', confirming both replication propagation and read-only enforcement.

overall_summary: All material outcomes of the task — PostgreSQL streaming replication installed and configured across node1 (primary), node2 and node3 (standbys), with standbys provisioned via pg_basebackup, streaming confirmed via pg_stat_replication, and a primary write observed to propagate to both standbys while direct standby writes were rejected — are directly and coherently supported by the captured evidence. The independently required node-restart evidence protocol was also executed completely and consistently: standbys were restarted first, then the primary, each showing a pre-restart boot ID, a restart acknowledgement, a distinct post-restart boot ID matching the fixed after-executor snapshot, and confirmed recovery of PostgreSQL, replication streaming, and data (including a post-restart write visible on both standbys), demonstrating the configuration survives a full-cluster restart.
limitations: The task instruction itself does not require restart/reboot survival; the restart evidence is supplemental per the provider-wide protocol and was used here only to corroborate operational health, not as a required task outcome.

One transient pg_basebackup failure due to a slot-name conflict occurred on both standbys before the successful run; it was immediately self-corrected and left no residue, but it does reflect a minor sequencing oversight (manually pre-creating slots then also requesting slot creation via pg_basebackup -C).

operational_hygiene.summary: Data directories on node2/node3 were wiped (cmd-6340cc35a90343d1, cmd-ff23976437554860) before pg_basebackup — a necessary and expected step to convert freshly-initialized standalone clusters into standbys, not unnecessary residue. An initial pg_basebackup attempt with -C on both nodes (cmd-2c3ec5d9d3144ad9, cmd-4c0b71da328a40fc) failed because the replication slots already existed (created manually beforehand); the failure removed its own partial data directory contents and the executor immediately retried without -C successfully (cmd-4105423fde86443d, cmd-be59bb32ae034773). This was a bounded, self-correcting troubleshooting step with no lasting residue. The mandatory node-restart evidence protocol (standbys first, primary last) is fully documented with pre-restart boot IDs, reboot acknowledgements, changed post-restart boot IDs, and confirmed service/data/replication recovery on all three nodes, consistent with the fixed after-executor snapshot boot IDs. No failed services, no abandoned files, and no unnecessary exposure were observed in the after-executor snapshot beyond the expected new PostgreSQL 5432 listeners.
